section_summary: This section begins with a 1930 Embassy report surveying the history, organization, circulation, ethics, political influence, management, and legal regulation of the Japanese press, including profiles of leading newspapers and a translation of the 1909 Press Law. Later documents update the survey for 1932, emphasizing changes in newspaper ownership, political affiliations, militarism, and attitudes toward the United States. A 1933 despatch records the Foreign Office-backed reorganization of the Japan Times and Mail, while 1934 materials warn that the proposed merger of the Rengo and Nippon Dempo agencies could facilitate centralized government control and propaganda.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 55 transmitting “The Japanese Press”
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits an Embassy staff report entitled “The Japanese Press.”
subfiles.summary: Ambassador William R. Castle Jr. forwards a report on the Japanese press prepared by a member of his staff. The report is included as the despatch's sole enclosure.

subfiles.title: The Japanese Press
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo; attributed by the Department to William T. Turner
subfiles.about: Surveys the development, organization, influence, ethics, economics, and principal institutions of the Japanese newspaper press.
subfiles.summary: The report traces Japanese journalism from the late shogunate and early Meiji period through the emergence of large metropolitan dailies in Tokyo and Osaka. It discusses circulation, page composition, advertising, labor-intensive typesetting, sensationalism, alleged blackmail, civic activities, and the press's increasing power over public opinion and government policy. It also examines official censorship, financial organization, political independence, and weak editorial coordination. An extensive appendix profiles major Tokyo and Osaka newspapers, listing their ownership, capital, circulation, executives, editors, stockholders, political tendencies, and readerships.

subfiles.title: The Press Law
subfiles.doc_type: translation of statute appended to report
subfiles.from: Japanese Government; English translation included by the American Embassy
subfiles.about: Provides an English translation of Japan's 1909 Press Law governing newspaper registration, financial guarantees, corrections, prohibited content, seizure, and punishment.
subfiles.summary: The statute defines newspapers and establishes eligibility, registration, publication, staffing, and deposit requirements. It requires delivery of copies to government and prosecutorial offices and provides a right of correction or contradiction. It restricts publication of judicial, official, military, naval, and foreign-affairs information and authorizes suppression, confiscation, and import bans for material deemed harmful to public order or morals. Articles 28 through 43, concerning punishments, are omitted from the translation.

subfiles.title: Memorandum concerning the Embassy report on the Japanese press
subfiles.about: Recommends recognition of William T. Turner for his work on the Embassy's Japanese press report.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes the report sent with Despatch No. 55 as excellent. It suggests that an appropriate notation be placed on Third Secretary William T. Turner's efficiency record because his initials appear on the report's carbon copies.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 49 praising “The Japanese Press”
subfiles.from: Secretary of State, signed for by Wilbur J. Carr
subfiles.to: William R. Castle Jr., American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Commends the Embassy's report on the Japanese press and its reference appendix.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that it has read the report with interest and considers it excellent, concise, and adequate. It particularly praises the appendix describing the principal Japanese newspapers as a useful reference work.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 198
subfiles.about: Notes that Despatch No. 198 updates the 1930 survey because the political character of Japan's newspapers had become more important during the international crisis.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that changes in affiliations, policies, and political complexions made a revision of the 1930 report necessary. It characterizes the new despatch chiefly as a reference document.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 198: Affiliations, Policies and Political Complexion of the Principal Newspapers in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits an updated résumé of major Japanese newspapers and their political affiliations and biases.
subfiles.summary: Grew explains that changes in ownership and affiliation since the March 1930 survey require a revised account, especially amid the current international crisis. He emphasizes that the Osaka Asahi–Tokyo Asahi and Osaka Mainichi–Tokyo Nichinichi combinations are headquartered in Osaka and remain independent of political parties and government obligations. Copies were also directed to American posts in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenyang, and Harbin.

subfiles.title: Newspapers in Japan
subfiles.about: Updates the ownership, management, editorial positions, readerships, and influence of leading Japanese- and English-language newspapers.
subfiles.summary: The résumé ranks newspapers approximately by size and influence and compares several Japanese papers with prominent American and British publications. It describes the Asahi combination as conservative and anti-militarist, the Mainichi group as more popular and sensational, the Jiji Shimpo as business-oriented and pro-American, and several smaller papers as nationalist, anti-American, scandal-driven, or tied to political parties. It also examines the Japan Advertiser, Mainichi English edition, Japan Times and Mail, and Japan Chronicle. The account repeatedly assesses the newspapers' positions on militarism, the Manchurian dispute, the League of Nations, and relations with the United States.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 249
subfiles.about: Calls attention to the change in ownership and management of the Japan Times and Mail.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports that the Japan Times and Mail changed hands on January 1, 1933, with Hitoshi Ashida becoming publisher and editor. It recommends that the accompanying three-page despatch be read in full.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 249: Change in Ownership and Management of the Japan Times and Mail
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the reorganization of the Japan Times and Mail under Hitoshi Ashida and the Japanese Foreign Office's concealed financial control.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that former diplomat and Seiyukai Diet member Hitoshi Ashida became publisher and editor on January 1, with Yoshio Nitobe as managing editor. He reviews Ashida's liberal and League-friendly statements while noting his closeness to the militarist Foreign Office official Toshio Shiratori. The despatch states that the Foreign Office forced the sale by withdrawing its subsidy and then became, according to Shiratori, the newspaper's real largest owner. The new management publicly promised accurate news, liberal constitutionalism, international justice, and international amity.

subfiles.title: New Year's message to Hitoshi Ashida
subfiles.doc_type: letter, copy enclosed with Despatch No. 249
subfiles.about: Offers good wishes for Ashida's editorship and urges constructive optimism and international cooperation in 1933.
subfiles.summary: Grew congratulates Ashida on assuming the editorship of the Japan Times and describes it as an opportunity for constructive service. Reflecting on the economic hardship and international problems of 1932, he advocates optimism, confidence, hard work, friendship, and cooperation among nations.

subfiles.title: Hitoshi Ashida's reply to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.doc_type: letter, copy enclosed with Despatch No. 249
subfiles.from: Hitoshi Ashida, Japan Times, Hibiya Park, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador
subfiles.about: Thanks Grew for his New Year's message and promises to pursue the ideals expressed in it.
subfiles.summary: Ashida says he will proudly print Grew's letter in the first issue of the Japan Times under his direction. He accepts Grew's sentiments as an inspiring standard while asking indulgence if the newspaper initially falls short of their shared ideals.

subfiles.title: Report on the proposed amalgamation of Rengo and Nippon Dempo
subfiles.about: Outlines a Foreign Office-supported plan to merge Japan's two principal news agencies into a government-controlled organization.
subfiles.summary: The report says that Rengo and Nippon Dempo may be reorganized into a single agency capitalized at five million yen. Its head would be a government official assisted by military and naval representatives, while most existing personnel would remain. The writer warns that eliminating competition would give the government immense propaganda power and further reduce the reliability of Japanese news.

subfiles.title: Document File Note cross-referencing Despatch No. 1007
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to Despatch No. 1007 in file 894.00 P.R./82 for material on increasing Japanese government interference with the press.
subfiles.summary: The file note identifies a despatch from Japan by Grew dated October 11, 1934. Its stated subject is the Japanese Government's increasing tendency to interfere with the press.

subfiles.title: The Press
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Warns that government pressure on the press and the proposed Rengo–Nippon Dempo consolidation may be intended to control news during the anticipated crisis of 1935-1936.
subfiles.summary: The extract describes signs that the Japanese Government is increasingly interfering with the press, both to suppress politically unwelcome material and to curb sensational reports that might embarrass Japan internationally. It argues that the stated economic reasons for merging Rengo and Nippon Dempo probably conceal a desire for stricter control over incoming and outgoing news. The prospective goal is portrayed as official control capable of ensuring that only an approved Japanese viewpoint is circulated at home and abroad during the expected 1935-1936 crisis.
